medical.title: Early axial spondyloarthritis diagnosis linked to lower long-term spinal damage
medical.summary: Early axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), with a duration of no more than two years of axial symptoms, is associated with lower long-term spinal structural damage, according to a study published online Sept. 18 in Arthritis & Rheumatology.

medical.title: Drug tapering noninferior to treatment continuation for rheumatoid arthritis with low disease activity
medical.summary: For patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) with sustained low disease activity (LDA), structured tapering of biologic or targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (b/tsDMARDs) is noninferior to treatment continuation for maintaining disease control over 24 weeks, according to a study published online Oct. 6 in Arthritis & Rheumatology.

medical.title: Toddler EEG study shows why story time and playtime really matter
medical.summary: The everyday moments parents spend reading books, solving puzzles and playing with their toddlers may do more than create memories. New research shows these simple interactions engage young brains in ways that screen time cannot.

medical.title: Marijuana for insomnia? What the latest evidence says
medical.summary: If you struggle with insomnia, could medical marijuana help you get a better night's sleep?

medical.title: Alzheimer's blood biomarker tracks brain amyloid similarly across racial groups, study finds
medical.summary: A large global study provides new evidence supporting the use of blood biomarkers in an Alzheimer's clinical trial to screen for elevated brain amyloid levels among potential participants who are cognitively unimpaired. The findings, published in JAMA Neurology, show that the relationship between blood biomarker levels and brain amyloid was largely similar across racial groups.

medical.title: Arizona's controlled substances law worked, research finds
medical.summary: In 2018, Arizona lawmakers began requiring clinicians who prescribe high doses of opioids to also prescribe naloxone, the overdose-reversal medication commonly known by the brand name Narcan.

medical.title: What doctors want women to know about menopause and heart health
medical.summary: An estimated 6,000 women enter menopause every day in the United States, according to the National Institutes of Health. Yet many are surprised to learn that the years surrounding menopause can influence everything from sleep and mood to heart and long-term health and quality of life.

medical.title: Opioid prescriptions during pregnancy linked to higher rates of childhood hospital admission
medical.summary: Children whose mothers received opioid prescriptions during pregnancy have a higher rate of hospital admission in childhood than unexposed children, including unexposed siblings, according to a new study published in the open-access journal PLOS Medicine by Dong Keon Yon of Kyung Hee University College of Medicine, South Korea, and colleagues.

medical.title: Smartwatch can help screen for obstructive sleep apnea
medical.summary: New research suggests that a consumer smartwatch can help identify adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea, offering a way to screen for a common sleep disorder that often goes undiagnosed.

medical.title: Patients engage with epilepsy monitor in real time, improving seizure detection
medical.summary: A team has built an AI-based interface that enables real-time communication between patients and epilepsy monitoring devices. As part of a small clinical study at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, patients used a smartphone application to inquire about their own physiological data and received accurate information in response. In turn, the system learned from patient feedback to improve seizure detection, ultimately reducing its false alarms by about 80%. The research is published in Nature Medicine.

medical.title: Ketamine relieves pain without 'disconnecting' consciousness, study finds
medical.summary: An imaging study in humans led by Tel Aviv University's Institute for Psychedelic Research, in collaboration with TAU-affiliated Tel Aviv Medical Center (Ichilov), found that the pain relief provided by ketamine does not result from the sense of dissociation—a detachment from oneself, body or surroundings, induced by the drug. The findings, indicating that pain relief and the effect on consciousness are based on different brain mechanisms, may help in developing treatments that provide the benefits of ketamine while reducing its psychological side effects.

medical.title: New paper outlines growing role of interventional radiology in liver cancer treatment
medical.summary: Interventional radiologists (IRs) provide patients with primary and secondary liver cancer with high-quality, high-impact care in a more cost-efficient way than other specialties, according to a study published online in the Journal of Vascular and Interventional Radiology.

medical.title: General dietary interventions may matter more than specific habits before bariatric surgery, study shows
medical.summary: People preparing for metabolic-bariatric surgery may eat quite differently from one another, but those differences do not necessarily translate into different measures of cardiometabolic health, according to a new Concordia study. The researchers say the findings could help health professionals and patients make informed choices about lifestyle and eating habits in the lead-up to surgery—and earlier.

medical.title: Privacy-preserving training could expand medical AI for children while keeping data local
medical.summary: In the field of radiology, AI models have the potential to improve imaging analysis, speed up diagnoses and catch errors that might otherwise be missed. But the vast majority of these models are trained on adult data and don't translate well to infants and children, keeping these advances out of reach of neonatal and pediatric care.

medical.title: Protein reins in intestinal inflammation by curbing an overactive immune signal
medical.summary: A preclinical study by researchers at UT Southwestern Medical Center has discovered how a protein called ZBTB44 helps prevent excessive immune activity that can cause inflammation in the colon, the main section of the large intestine. The findings, published in Nature Immunology, may help explain how immune responses go awry in a range of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.

medical.title: Nicotine pouches, vaping or cigarettes: Which nicotine product is actually the least harmful?
medical.summary: "Do you smoke cigarettes?" I asked my patient during a recent clinic appointment.

medical.title: Does lithium in drinking water cause a rare heart condition?
medical.summary: Children living in areas with higher levels of lithium in drinking water were more likely to be diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, a rare heart condition that can cause a dangerously fast heartbeat, according to a new study led by UC San Francisco researchers.

medical.title: First case of teeth growing out of an eye socket—what you need to know about 'ectopic teeth'
medical.summary: A 16-year-old boy in India has had a tooth removed from his left eye socket, between the eyelid and the eyebrow. He had noticed a painless swelling for about a month but was only taken to a hospital when two hard, whitish points began poking through. A scan revealed a fully formed canine tooth—an extremely unusual example of an ectopic tooth.

medical.title: Targeted radioactive therapy may help delay spread of recurrent prostate cancer
medical.summary: Adding the targeted radioactive drug 177Lu-PNT2002 to stereotactic body radiation therapy, or SBRT, may help keep recurrent prostate cancer under control longer than SBRT alone, according to new research led by investigators at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

medical.title: Tumor suppressor gene mutations trigger immune activation in early oral cancer
medical.summary: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) frequently develops in the oral and upper aerodigestive regions following chronic exposure to mutagenic factors such as tobacco, alcohol and betel nut. Alterations in the tumor suppressor genes TP53 and CDKN2A are among the most common genetic changes in HNSCC and often occur together in the same tumor. However, the consequences of these combined alterations during the early stages of oral carcinogenesis remain poorly understood.

medical.title: Earlier menopause linked to faster biological aging, study finds
medical.summary: The age at which a woman experiences menopause and her reproductive history may be associated with how quickly she ages biologically, according to a study led by researchers from the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine).

medical.title: Q&A: Expert discusses Russian plague scare
medical.summary: The reported death of 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute in Shelekhov, Siberia, Russia, has raised questions about a possible exposure to pneumonic plague and prompted calls for greater transparency. Yersinia pestis is a gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium that causes plague.

medical.title: Triple-action drug retatrutide delivers major weight loss for people with diabetes, Phase III trial finds
medical.summary: A recent Phase III clinical trial, TRIUMPH-2, evaluated the efficacy and safety of retatrutide, a triple receptor agonist and experimental once-weekly injection being developed to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes. What sets it apart from drugs such as semaglutide (Wegovy), which targets one hormone, and tirzepatide (Zepbound), which targets two, is its ability to activate three hormone receptors at once.

medical.title: Prince William launches kit to help communities prepare for emergencies
medical.summary: The free, how-to resource shows people how to build resilience in their communities The post Prince William launches kit to help communities prepare for emergencies appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Leucine does more than build muscle. It powers up your cells
medical.summary: The essential amino acid leucine can boost cellular energy production by protecting key proteins on mitochondria from being destroyed. The discovery reveals a new connection between nutrition and metabolism that could eventually lead to new approaches for metabolic disorders and cancer.

science.title: Newly discovered antiviral system in bacteria is 'strangest of its kind'
science.summary: Researchers at Gladstone Institutes have uncovered an unusual bacterial immune system that operates in reverse of known defenses. The discovery, published in Molecular Cell, details the mechanics of "type VI retrons"—a counterintuitive class of bacterial defenses. More than just a biological curiosity, decoding these complex systems provides a molecular blueprint that scientists can adapt to engineer more efficient DNA-editing tools for human health and therapies.

science.title: NASA JPL testing readies Voyager technologies lander for moon mission
science.summary: A commercial lander that will be at the forefront of NASA's efforts to establish a moon base, humanity's first lunar outpost, has passed a series of critical tests at the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The tests simulated the extreme temperatures and vacuum of space, as well as the intense shaking and ear-splitting roar of launch. Results show that Voyager Technologies' Griffin Mission One (Griffin-1) spacecraft is ready to survive the rigors of space exploration.

science.title: Chemical surroundings, not size alone, help glucose-processing enzyme stay active as temperatures rise
science.summary: Cells must produce energy despite changing conditions. But what keeps metabolic enzymes functional during temperature fluctuations? A team led by professor Simon Ebbinghaus and Dr. Harshita Rastogi at Ruhr University Bochum and the Research Center for Chemical Sciences and Sustainability investigated this question using the platelet isoform of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFKP), a central enzyme in glucose metabolism.

science.title: Americans are stressed about grocery prices, so why do they toss or overlook so much 'misfit' food?
science.summary: There's a paradox that drives the shopping decisions of many Americans: Almost three-quarters say they're feeling stressed out about skyrocketing grocery bills. But they keep discarding large quantities of food that's safe to eat, from crooked carrots to surplus yogurt to "best before" items pulled from shelves early.

science.title: Across the US, people don't want data centers coming to their communities
science.summary: Regardless of their views on politics or climate change, most Americans oppose the development of data centers in their communities.

science.title: Winged insect evolution: New evidence sheds light on century-old debate
science.summary: A new study combining genomic analyses and fossil evidence sheds light on the century-old "Palaeoptera Problem," a longstanding debate over the evolutionary relationships among major groups of winged insects.

science.title: Variations in the human vocal tract could have influenced language diversity
science.summary: The anatomical differences in our vocal tracts could be one of the sources of our Tower of Babel—the vast difference in languages spoken around the world, according to a study published in the open-access journal PLOS Biology by Steven Moran and Tiena Danner from the University of Neuchâtel, Switzerland, and colleagues.

science.title: 'Atmospheric rivers' helped open a Portugal-sized hole in Antarctica's winter sea ice
science.summary: Polynyas are patches of open water surrounded by sea ice, where heat and moisture can pass freely between the ocean and atmosphere. In August 2024, a vast polynya opened up in Breid Bay, off the coast of East Antarctica, in the depths of winter. The region had stayed ice-covered at this time of year ever since satellite records began in 1979.

science.title: Colorado River drought drives unprecedented pattern of groundwater loss
science.summary: Declining Colorado River flows and falling water levels at Lake Powell and Lake Mead are highly visible signs of the Southwestern megadrought.

science.title: New solar model maps sun more accurately by checking far-side activity
science.summary: A Southwest Research Institute (SwRI)-led team has developed an improved model for predicting solar events that incorporates activity on the far side of the sun. The team studied near-simultaneous maps of the whole solar surface from 2010 to 2014, combining Earth observations with data from space-based assets showing the opposite side. The resulting framework constructs surface flux transport (SFT) models that are more complete and accurate than any previous model.

science.title: How literature can inspire us to forgive
science.summary: A story that places us inside the mind of a character who is remorseful about causing harm can inspire forgiveness for that fictional bad act, a new study finds.

science.title: Sexual violence survivors often expect systems to fail or harm them, study finds
science.summary: University students who are survivors of sexual violence are forced to perform a constant, exhausting "calculus"—weighing risks, safety, stigma, emotional costs, institutional consequences and likelihood of being believed—when deciding whether and how to seek help.

science.title: A small RNA switch with huge potential opens up new possibilities for synthetic biology
science.summary: An international research team led by TU Darmstadt Professor Beatrix Süß, working in close collaboration with partners in Germany and Denmark, has elucidated how an RNA switch newly developed at TU Darmstadt recognizes the antibiotic doxycycline and thereby selectively activates or deactivates gene expression. This makes doxycycline a promising basis for synthetic biology and, potentially, for gene therapies as well. The team recently published its findings in Nature Communications.

science.title: A closer look at hard-to-see cells could answer new questions about nerve damage and recovery
science.summary: Under the microscope, mitochondria inside healthy terminal Schwann cells form a web of interconnected branches, with tiny doughnut-shaped loops appearing near where the cells branch and split.

science.title: Air conditioners contribute to climate change—this 40‑year‑old treaty aims to limit the harm
science.summary: As temperatures broke records this summer, sales of air-conditioning units soared. But this technology can compound climate change.

science.title: Feeling undervalued emerges as strongest link to women leaving academia, survey finds
science.summary: Women leave academia at higher rates than men, contributing to consistent gender imbalances at senior levels. Interventions often target work-life balance and motherhood.

science.title: Powerful X-rays reveal unexpected roles for water in enzymes linked to cancer and penicillin
science.summary: In biology, a group of enzymes called 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases is responsible for catalyzing a wide range of reactions that play a role in everything from how genetic code is used by cells to the synthesis of antibiotics.

science.title: Boys' lower regard for school effort may help explain academic gender gap
science.summary: A survey of 15-year-olds around the world suggests that the underperformance of boys in education may be linked to gendered cultural attitudes about whether it is important to try hard at school.

science.title: Recycled fertilizers from sanitation systems are as effective as conventional fertilizers, study finds
science.summary: Agriculture depends on a reliable supply of nutrients. Phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium, for example, are indispensable for agricultural crop production. However, natural reserves are limited, vary greatly in regional availability or are very energy-intensive to extract.

science.title: Structure in the unstructured: New phenomenon discovered in the solar wind
science.summary: Turbulence is ubiquitous and occurs every day, such as when milk is stirred into coffee or in the stormy motions of the ocean and the atmosphere. Media in space and astrophysical systems can also develop turbulence, but the physics is different because the medium is in an ionized state (known as the plasma state) and the flow motion is strongly coupled to electromagnetic fields. Furthermore, space plasma is collisionless because the medium is so dilute that the particles do not collide with each other.

science.title: Copper-resistant bacteria complicate efforts to keep ship hulls clean
science.summary: Marine bacteria have evolved to bypass the copper-based coatings applied to ship hulls to stop the growth of barnacles, algae and other marine life. This necessitates new methods for managing biofouling—the unwanted accumulation of marine organisms—on ship hulls.

science.title: How much training is too much for a racehorse? New bone research has some answers
science.summary: The old "more is better" mindset in racehorse training is changing. And with no link identified between higher racehorse training workloads and a trainer's success, there's a big opportunity to change things.

environment.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea

The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

environment.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
environment.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

environment.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
environment.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

environment.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
environment.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

environment.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
environment.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

environment.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
environment.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.

mix_items.title: Newly discovered antiviral system in bacteria is 'strangest of its kind'
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Gladstone Institutes have uncovered an unusual bacterial immune system that operates in reverse of known defenses. The discovery, published in Molecular Cell, details the mechanics of "type VI retrons"—a counterintuitive class of bacterial defenses. More than just a biological curiosity, decoding these complex systems provides a molecular blueprint that scientists can adapt to engineer more efficient DNA-editing tools for human health and therapies.

mix_items.title: NASA JPL testing readies Voyager technologies lander for moon mission
mix_items.summary: A commercial lander that will be at the forefront of NASA's efforts to establish a moon base, humanity's first lunar outpost, has passed a series of critical tests at the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The tests simulated the extreme temperatures and vacuum of space, as well as the intense shaking and ear-splitting roar of launch. Results show that Voyager Technologies' Griffin Mission One (Griffin-1) spacecraft is ready to survive the rigors of space exploration.

mix_items.title: Toddler EEG study shows why story time and playtime really matter
mix_items.summary: The everyday moments parents spend reading books, solving puzzles and playing with their toddlers may do more than create memories. New research shows these simple interactions engage young brains in ways that screen time cannot.

mix_items.title: Chemical surroundings, not size alone, help glucose-processing enzyme stay active as temperatures rise
mix_items.summary: Cells must produce energy despite changing conditions. But what keeps metabolic enzymes functional during temperature fluctuations? A team led by professor Simon Ebbinghaus and Dr. Harshita Rastogi at Ruhr University Bochum and the Research Center for Chemical Sciences and Sustainability investigated this question using the platelet isoform of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFKP), a central enzyme in glucose metabolism.

mix_items.title: Americans are stressed about grocery prices, so why do they toss or overlook so much 'misfit' food?
mix_items.summary: There's a paradox that drives the shopping decisions of many Americans: Almost three-quarters say they're feeling stressed out about skyrocketing grocery bills. But they keep discarding large quantities of food that's safe to eat, from crooked carrots to surplus yogurt to "best before" items pulled from shelves early.

mix_items.title: Winged insect evolution: New evidence sheds light on century-old debate
mix_items.summary: A new study combining genomic analyses and fossil evidence sheds light on the century-old "Palaeoptera Problem," a longstanding debate over the evolutionary relationships among major groups of winged insects.

mix_items.title: Alzheimer's blood biomarker tracks brain amyloid similarly across racial groups, study finds
mix_items.summary: A large global study provides new evidence supporting the use of blood biomarkers in an Alzheimer's clinical trial to screen for elevated brain amyloid levels among potential participants who are cognitively unimpaired. The findings, published in JAMA Neurology, show that the relationship between blood biomarker levels and brain amyloid was largely similar across racial groups.

mix_items.title: Variations in the human vocal tract could have influenced language diversity
mix_items.summary: The anatomical differences in our vocal tracts could be one of the sources of our Tower of Babel—the vast difference in languages spoken around the world, according to a study published in the open-access journal PLOS Biology by Steven Moran and Tiena Danner from the University of Neuchâtel, Switzerland, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: What doctors want women to know about menopause and heart health
mix_items.summary: An estimated 6,000 women enter menopause every day in the United States, according to the National Institutes of Health. Yet many are surprised to learn that the years surrounding menopause can influence everything from sleep and mood to heart and long-term health and quality of life.

mix_items.title: Opioid prescriptions during pregnancy linked to higher rates of childhood hospital admission
mix_items.summary: Children whose mothers received opioid prescriptions during pregnancy have a higher rate of hospital admission in childhood than unexposed children, including unexposed siblings, according to a new study published in the open-access journal PLOS Medicine by Dong Keon Yon of Kyung Hee University College of Medicine, South Korea, and colleagues.

mix_items.summary: New research suggests that a consumer smartwatch can help identify adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea, offering a way to screen for a common sleep disorder that often goes undiagnosed.

mix_items.title: Patients engage with epilepsy monitor in real time, improving seizure detection
mix_items.summary: A team has built an AI-based interface that enables real-time communication between patients and epilepsy monitoring devices. As part of a small clinical study at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, patients used a smartphone application to inquire about their own physiological data and received accurate information in response. In turn, the system learned from patient feedback to improve seizure detection, ultimately reducing its false alarms by about 80%. The research is published in Nature Medicine.

mix_items.title: 'Atmospheric rivers' helped open a Portugal-sized hole in Antarctica's winter sea ice
mix_items.summary: Polynyas are patches of open water surrounded by sea ice, where heat and moisture can pass freely between the ocean and atmosphere. In August 2024, a vast polynya opened up in Breid Bay, off the coast of East Antarctica, in the depths of winter. The region had stayed ice-covered at this time of year ever since satellite records began in 1979.

mix_items.title: Colorado River drought drives unprecedented pattern of groundwater loss
mix_items.summary: Declining Colorado River flows and falling water levels at Lake Powell and Lake Mead are highly visible signs of the Southwestern megadrought.

mix_items.title: New solar model maps sun more accurately by checking far-side activity
mix_items.summary: A Southwest Research Institute (SwRI)-led team has developed an improved model for predicting solar events that incorporates activity on the far side of the sun. The team studied near-simultaneous maps of the whole solar surface from 2010 to 2014, combining Earth observations with data from space-based assets showing the opposite side. The resulting framework constructs surface flux transport (SFT) models that are more complete and accurate than any previous model.

mix_items.title: How literature can inspire us to forgive
mix_items.summary: A story that places us inside the mind of a character who is remorseful about causing harm can inspire forgiveness for that fictional bad act, a new study finds.

mix_items.title: Ketamine relieves pain without 'disconnecting' consciousness, study finds
mix_items.summary: An imaging study in humans led by Tel Aviv University's Institute for Psychedelic Research, in collaboration with TAU-affiliated Tel Aviv Medical Center (Ichilov), found that the pain relief provided by ketamine does not result from the sense of dissociation—a detachment from oneself, body or surroundings, induced by the drug. The findings, indicating that pain relief and the effect on consciousness are based on different brain mechanisms, may help in developing treatments that provide the benefits of ketamine while reducing its psychological side effects.

mix_items.title: New paper outlines growing role of interventional radiology in liver cancer treatment
mix_items.summary: Interventional radiologists (IRs) provide patients with primary and secondary liver cancer with high-quality, high-impact care in a more cost-efficient way than other specialties, according to a study published online in the Journal of Vascular and Interventional Radiology.

mix_items.title: Sexual violence survivors often expect systems to fail or harm them, study finds
mix_items.summary: University students who are survivors of sexual violence are forced to perform a constant, exhausting "calculus"—weighing risks, safety, stigma, emotional costs, institutional consequences and likelihood of being believed—when deciding whether and how to seek help.

mix_items.title: A small RNA switch with huge potential opens up new possibilities for synthetic biology
mix_items.summary: An international research team led by TU Darmstadt Professor Beatrix Süß, working in close collaboration with partners in Germany and Denmark, has elucidated how an RNA switch newly developed at TU Darmstadt recognizes the antibiotic doxycycline and thereby selectively activates or deactivates gene expression. This makes doxycycline a promising basis for synthetic biology and, potentially, for gene therapies as well. The team recently published its findings in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: General dietary interventions may matter more than specific habits before bariatric surgery, study shows
mix_items.summary: People preparing for metabolic-bariatric surgery may eat quite differently from one another, but those differences do not necessarily translate into different measures of cardiometabolic health, according to a new Concordia study. The researchers say the findings could help health professionals and patients make informed choices about lifestyle and eating habits in the lead-up to surgery—and earlier.

mix_items.title: A closer look at hard-to-see cells could answer new questions about nerve damage and recovery
mix_items.summary: Under the microscope, mitochondria inside healthy terminal Schwann cells form a web of interconnected branches, with tiny doughnut-shaped loops appearing near where the cells branch and split.

mix_items.title: Privacy-preserving training could expand medical AI for children while keeping data local
mix_items.summary: In the field of radiology, AI models have the potential to improve imaging analysis, speed up diagnoses and catch errors that might otherwise be missed. But the vast majority of these models are trained on adult data and don't translate well to infants and children, keeping these advances out of reach of neonatal and pediatric care.

mix_items.title: Protein reins in intestinal inflammation by curbing an overactive immune signal
mix_items.summary: A preclinical study by researchers at UT Southwestern Medical Center has discovered how a protein called ZBTB44 helps prevent excessive immune activity that can cause inflammation in the colon, the main section of the large intestine. The findings, published in Nature Immunology, may help explain how immune responses go awry in a range of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.

mix_items.title: Air conditioners contribute to climate change—this 40‑year‑old treaty aims to limit the harm
mix_items.summary: As temperatures broke records this summer, sales of air-conditioning units soared. But this technology can compound climate change.

mix_items.title: Nicotine pouches, vaping or cigarettes: Which nicotine product is actually the least harmful?
mix_items.summary: "Do you smoke cigarettes?" I asked my patient during a recent clinic appointment.

mix_items.title: Does lithium in drinking water cause a rare heart condition?
mix_items.summary: Children living in areas with higher levels of lithium in drinking water were more likely to be diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, a rare heart condition that can cause a dangerously fast heartbeat, according to a new study led by UC San Francisco researchers.

mix_items.title: Feeling undervalued emerges as strongest link to women leaving academia, survey finds
mix_items.summary: Women leave academia at higher rates than men, contributing to consistent gender imbalances at senior levels. Interventions often target work-life balance and motherhood.

mix_items.title: First case of teeth growing out of an eye socket—what you need to know about 'ectopic teeth'
mix_items.summary: A 16-year-old boy in India has had a tooth removed from his left eye socket, between the eyelid and the eyebrow. He had noticed a painless swelling for about a month but was only taken to a hospital when two hard, whitish points began poking through. A scan revealed a fully formed canine tooth—an extremely unusual example of an ectopic tooth.

mix_items.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
mix_items.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

mix_items.title: Targeted radioactive therapy may help delay spread of recurrent prostate cancer
mix_items.summary: Adding the targeted radioactive drug 177Lu-PNT2002 to stereotactic body radiation therapy, or SBRT, may help keep recurrent prostate cancer under control longer than SBRT alone, according to new research led by investigators at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

mix_items.title: Powerful X-rays reveal unexpected roles for water in enzymes linked to cancer and penicillin
mix_items.summary: In biology, a group of enzymes called 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases is responsible for catalyzing a wide range of reactions that play a role in everything from how genetic code is used by cells to the synthesis of antibiotics.

mix_items.title: Boys' lower regard for school effort may help explain academic gender gap
mix_items.summary: A survey of 15-year-olds around the world suggests that the underperformance of boys in education may be linked to gendered cultural attitudes about whether it is important to try hard at school.

mix_items.title: Tumor suppressor gene mutations trigger immune activation in early oral cancer
mix_items.summary: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) frequently develops in the oral and upper aerodigestive regions following chronic exposure to mutagenic factors such as tobacco, alcohol and betel nut. Alterations in the tumor suppressor genes TP53 and CDKN2A are among the most common genetic changes in HNSCC and often occur together in the same tumor. However, the consequences of these combined alterations during the early stages of oral carcinogenesis remain poorly understood.

mix_items.title: Recycled fertilizers from sanitation systems are as effective as conventional fertilizers, study finds
mix_items.summary: Agriculture depends on a reliable supply of nutrients. Phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium, for example, are indispensable for agricultural crop production. However, natural reserves are limited, vary greatly in regional availability or are very energy-intensive to extract.

mix_items.title: Structure in the unstructured: New phenomenon discovered in the solar wind
mix_items.summary: Turbulence is ubiquitous and occurs every day, such as when milk is stirred into coffee or in the stormy motions of the ocean and the atmosphere. Media in space and astrophysical systems can also develop turbulence, but the physics is different because the medium is in an ionized state (known as the plasma state) and the flow motion is strongly coupled to electromagnetic fields. Furthermore, space plasma is collisionless because the medium is so dilute that the particles do not collide with each other.

mix_items.title: Earlier menopause linked to faster biological aging, study finds
mix_items.summary: The age at which a woman experiences menopause and her reproductive history may be associated with how quickly she ages biologically, according to a study led by researchers from the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine).

mix_items.title: Copper-resistant bacteria complicate efforts to keep ship hulls clean
mix_items.summary: Marine bacteria have evolved to bypass the copper-based coatings applied to ship hulls to stop the growth of barnacles, algae and other marine life. This necessitates new methods for managing biofouling—the unwanted accumulation of marine organisms—on ship hulls.

mix_items.title: How much training is too much for a racehorse? New bone research has some answers
mix_items.summary: The old "more is better" mindset in racehorse training is changing. And with no link identified between higher racehorse training workloads and a trainer's success, there's a big opportunity to change things.

mix_items.title: Q&A: Expert discusses Russian plague scare
mix_items.summary: The reported death of 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute in Shelekhov, Siberia, Russia, has raised questions about a possible exposure to pneumonic plague and prompted calls for greater transparency. Yersinia pestis is a gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium that causes plague.

mix_items.title: Triple-action drug retatrutide delivers major weight loss for people with diabetes, Phase III trial finds
mix_items.summary: A recent Phase III clinical trial, TRIUMPH-2, evaluated the efficacy and safety of retatrutide, a triple receptor agonist and experimental once-weekly injection being developed to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes. What sets it apart from drugs such as semaglutide (Wegovy), which targets one hormone, and tirzepatide (Zepbound), which targets two, is its ability to activate three hormone receptors at once.

mix_items.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
mix_items.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

mix_items.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
mix_items.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

mix_items.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
mix_items.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

mix_items.title: Prince William launches kit to help communities prepare for emergencies
mix_items.summary: The free, how-to resource shows people how to build resilience in their communities The post Prince William launches kit to help communities prepare for emergencies appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: Leucine does more than build muscle. It powers up your cells
mix_items.summary: The essential amino acid leucine can boost cellular energy production by protecting key proteins on mitochondria from being destroyed. The discovery reveals a new connection between nutrition and metabolism that could eventually lead to new approaches for metabolic disorders and cancer.

mix_items.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
mix_items.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

mix_items.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.
